cited_by.label: Isaiah 31 · Egypt Is Flesh, Not Spirit
Isaiah 31 · Egypt Is Flesh, Not Spirit

precepts.text: The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee and laughed thee to scorn. The angel of the Lord smote a hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians overnight, and Sennacherib returned to Nineveh, where his own sons killed him with the sword while he worshipped his god. You will not one-up God; he will one-up you, and that includes the online mockers of God's prophets.
precepts.point: Sennacherib king of Assyria took Judah's defenced cities and sent Rabshakeh to mock Hezekiah in the Jews' language, boasting that no god of any nation had delivered his land out of the king of Assyria's hand.
precepts.why:
Pride destroyed every kingdom on the earth, and Assyria is the first king in line. Sennacherib took all the defenced cities of Judah, then sent Rabshakeh, his herald, with big words: “What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?” When Hezekiah's men begged him to speak in the Syrian language so the people on the wall would not hear, he said he was sent to “the men that sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung, and drink their own piss with you.” Then he mocked the Lord himself: “Hath any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?” … “that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?” All that pride came out of the king of Assyria's mouth by way of his messenger.

God heard all that smack. “Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Whereas thou hast prayed to me against Sennacherib king of Assyria: This is the word which the Lord hath spoken concerning him; The virgin, the daughter of Zion, hath despised thee, and laughed thee to scorn; the daughter of Jerusalem hath shaken her head at thee.” She is laughing at this man's tough talk, the way a parent shakes their head when they told you not to do it and are about to whoop your ass. You are not going to one-up God, and that goes for everyone making videos mocking God's prophets. God will one-up you.

“For I will defend this city to save it for mine own sake, and for my servant David’s sake. Then the angel of the Lord went forth, and smote in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and fourscore and five thousand.” One of God's angels destroyed 185,000. The sun went down and they were all alive; at the crack of the morning, “they were all dead corpses.” Talking prideful against God, everybody had to die.

But God was hunting Sennacherib himself. “So Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, and went and returned, and dwelt at Nineveh.” He thought he got away. Then “as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god”, his own sons “smote him with the sword”, and they escaped into Armenia, and his other son Esarhaddon reigned in his stead and didn't even care.

Pride destroyed the king of Assyria, as “a man’s pride shall bring him low” in Proverbs 29. And it is the same line through every kingdom after him, Babylon, the Greeks, Rome and America: none is exempt from pride, and none is exempt from God destroying them for it.

precepts.text: Sennacherib mocks trust in Egypt, the broken reed, and dangles two thousand horses to turn the heart.
precepts.point: We honor the Most High with our lips, but when the oppressor offers gifts we turn away and serve our oppressor's will. When Sennacherib's servant Rabshakeh offered Hezekiah two thousand horses, it was the same trick, a gift to pull the heart off the Most High.

note.label: Isaiah 31: Egypt Is Flesh, Not Spirit

precepts.why:
Here is the going down to Egypt for help in the history. It was “in the fourteenth year of king Hezekiah, that Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defenced cities of Judah, and took them.” His servant Rabshakeh mocked the trust in Egypt: “Lo, thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt; whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all that trust in him.”

Then he dangled the gift: “Now therefore give pledges, I pray thee, to my master the king of Assyria, and I will give thee two thousand horses, if thou be able on thy part to set riders upon them.” Two thousand horses to stay on, the very horses and chariots Isaiah 31 says woe to. It was the same trick, a gift to pull the heart off the Most High. We honor him with our lips, but when the oppressor offers gifts we turn away and serve our oppressor’s will, instead of looking to the Holy One of Israel.

points: Sennacherib king of Assyria took Judah's defenced cities and sent Rabshakeh to mock Hezekiah in the Jews' language, boasting that no god of any nation had delivered his land out of the king of Assyria's hand.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the defended cities of Judah and took them. Assyria was the rod the Most High used to press Judah.
The king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a great army, and he stood by the conduit of the upper pool. Eliakim, Shebna the scribe, and Joah the recorder came out to meet him.
Rabshakeh challenges Hezekiah's confidence, asking in whom he trusts, and calls his words but vain words. He mocks any counsel or strength for war.

He warns against trusting in the staff of the broken reed of Egypt, which pierces the hand of the man who leans on it. Trusting Egypt instead of the Most High is the constant temptation set before Judah.

He twists Hezekiah's removal of the high places, claiming it offended the Most High, and boasts that even Assyria was sent by the Lord to destroy the land. He speaks as though the Most High is on his side.

Eliakim and Shebna and Joah ask Rabshakeh to speak in the Syrian language, which they understand, and not in the Jews' language in the ears of the people on the wall. They do not want the people to hear the threats.

Rabshakeh refuses, saying his master sent him to the men on the wall, who are the ones set to eat their own dung and drink their own piss with them. He deliberately speaks to frighten the common people.

Rabshakeh stands and cries with a loud voice in the Jews' language, telling the people not to let Hezekiah deceive them, for he cannot deliver them. He works to break the people's trust in their king.

He tells them not to let Hezekiah make them trust in the Most High to deliver the city, but to make an agreement with him and come out, promising each man his own vine and fig tree until he takes them to a land like their own. It is a bribe dressed up as mercy.

He lists the gods of Hamath, Arphad, and Sepharvaim, and asks whether any of them delivered their land or Samaria out of his hand, so that the Most High should deliver Jerusalem. He counts the living God as no better than the idols of the nations.
The people hold their peace and answer him not a word, for Hezekiah's commandment was to answer him not. They do not argue with the blasphemer.
Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and tell him the words of Rabshakeh. They bring the blasphemy before the king in mourning.
